description: We are passionate about space, coding and AI and we love turning ideas into projects. Last year, we worked on an artificial space station project that included 3D renders, animations, a gravity calculator and a Mars survival game. This year we want to use NASA data to explore Earth’s challenges and build something meaningful. We are interested in working with people who enjoy science, programming, data analysis and creative problem solving.
summary: NexusEarth is an interactive, bilingual platform for exploring how Earth’s environment changes across places and time. It brings together NASA and partner datasets—including temperature, precipitation, vegetation, soil moisture, terrestrial water storage, ozone, sea level, and SWOT lake observations—on a 3D globe. Users can switch visual map layers, explore available years, select a location or region, and view data series and trend statistics where the records support analysis. The platform distinguishes map visualization from statistical results and communicates data gaps and limitations to help users interpret findings responsibly. By making Earth-observation data easier to explore and compare, NexusEarth supports a clearer understanding of environmental change without presenting correlation as causation.
details:
NexusEarth is an interactive, bilingual Earth sciences platform developed for the competition titled "Be an Earth Systems Trend Detective!" It enables students and the general public to explore how environmental conditions change across space and time, visualized on a 3D globe. Users can search for a specific location or define an area, select from a variety of environmental variables, and subsequently examine relevant data series and trend statistics. Depending on the chosen data product, the platform offers capabilities for point-based analysis, regional sample estimations, or area-weighted polygon analysis for supported datasets and geometries regions.

NexusEarth integrates data from various sources into a single interface. NASA POWER provides daily temperature and corrected precipitation data, as well as air temperature and evapotranspiration energy flux data derived from MERRA-2. Google Earth Engine provides access to datasets such as MODIS Terra vegetation indices (MOD13Q1), SMAP near-surface soil moisture, GRACE/GRACE-FO terrestrial water storage anomalies, GPM IMERG precipitation rates, and TOMS/MERGED_V4 total column ozone. For sea-level analysis, the platform utilizes current NOAA CoastWatch satellite altimetry data; for comparisons covering earlier periods, it relies on HYCOM model outputs—which consist of modeled data—rather than direct satellite measurements. For specific supported regions, such as the Aral Sea and Lake Chad, SWOT lake surface elevation observations are obtained via the Hydrocron service, hosted by NASA’s PO.DAAC. Visual map layers provided by NASA GIBS are kept separate from the numerical data used in statistical analyses.

NexusEarth calculates the "Sen’s slope" for supported annual records and examines monotonic trends in the data using either the Mann-Kendall test (as modified by Hamed and Rao) or the classic Mann-Kendall test, depending on the specific case. In instances where the number of annual observations is insufficient or the data contains gaps, results regarding statistical significance are not provided. Since SWOT observations occur at irregular intervals, these data are presented using a descriptive approach rather than through long-term significance testing.

The platform’s frontend is developed using TypeScript, incorporating React, Vite, and CesiumJS technologies. The backend, built on Python FastAPI, connects to Google Earth Engine—as well as data services from NASA and other partners—to process data and perform statistical calculations. Additional features include annual comparisons for "Global Stories," GBIF biodiversity records for context, lagged correlation analysis, regional exposure summaries, curated examples, and the ability to export scientific information as a PDF.

The project’s innovative approach integrates diverse Earth observation datasets, trend analysis, and explanatory storytelling into an interactive 3D globe. This enables users to explore environmental patterns without the need to download large datasets or possess prior knowledge of specialized analysis software. Our goal is to help people investigate environmental change, understand the evidence, and ask better questions—not to present the platform as a forecasting tool or an emergency warning system.

During development, we took into account data sources, units, timeframes, spatial coverage, missing observations, and discrepancies between observed measurements and model outputs. Furthermore, in designing the platform for both beginners and more experienced users, we incorporated bilingual explanations, transparent methodologies, and clear statements regarding limitations—while also employing careful phrasing to avoid conflating correlation with causation.

Note: If you encounter an error while accessing the website due to your network, please try using a VPN and accessing it again.
